rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem: Name the extrinsic semiconductors formed when a pure germanium is doped with (i) a trivalent and (ii) pentavalent impurity. Draw the energy band diagrams of extrinsic semiconductors so formed.
rows.solution:
**Naming the two.**

| Dopant | Valency | Semiconductor formed | Majority carriers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trivalent — boron, aluminium, indium, gallium | 3 | **p-type** | holes |
| Pentavalent — phosphorus, arsenic, antimony, bismuth | 5 | **n-type** | electrons |

Germanium is tetravalent, so each atom needs four electrons to complete its covalent bonds with its four neighbours.

A **trivalent** dopant brings only three. One bond is left with a vacancy — a **hole** — which a neighbouring electron can move into, so the hole travels. The impurity is called an **acceptor**, because it accepts an electron to complete that bond.

A **pentavalent** dopant brings five. Four go into bonds and the fifth is left over, bound to its parent atom only weakly and free to wander with very little encouragement. The impurity is a **donor**.

**The energy band diagrams.**

Both are drawn with the valence band below, the conduction band above, and a gap \(E_g\) between them (\(0{\cdot}7\) eV for germanium). The doping does not change \(E_g\); it inserts a **new level inside the gap**, and where that level sits is the whole difference.

**n-type.** A **donor level \(E_D\)** appears just *below* the bottom of the conduction band, separated from it by only about \(0{\cdot}01\) eV in germanium. Mark it as a dashed line carrying the extra electrons. Because \(E_C - E_D \ll E_g\), thermal energy at room temperature \((kT \approx 0{\cdot}026\ \mathrm{eV})\) lifts essentially every one of those electrons into the conduction band. The conduction band is therefore well populated, while the valence band has lost almost nothing.

**p-type.** An **acceptor level \(E_A\)** appears just *above* the top of the valence band, by about \(0{\cdot}01\) to \(0{\cdot}05\) eV. Draw it as an empty dashed line. Valence electrons are thermally lifted into it, leaving **holes** behind in the valence band, which then carry the current. The conduction band stays nearly empty.

**The point the diagrams are meant to make.** Doping does not narrow the forbidden gap. It plants a level so close to one band edge that the *effective* energy a carrier must find drops from about \(0{\cdot}7\) eV to about \(0{\cdot}01\) eV — a factor of seventy, and since the carrier population depends on that energy exponentially, the conductivity rises by many orders of magnitude for one impurity atom in a million.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem:
The work function of a metal is 2.31 eV. Photoelectric emission occurs when light of frequency \(6.4 \times 10^{14}\) Hz is incident on the metal surface. Calculate :
(i) the energy of the incident radiation, (ii) the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron and (iii) the stopping potential of the surface.
rows.solution:
**(i) The energy of the incident radiation.**

\(E = h\nu = 6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34} \times 6{\cdot}4 \times 10^{14}\)

\(E = 4{\cdot}24 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\)

Converting to electronvolts, so that it can be set beside the work function:

\(E = \dfrac{4{\cdot}24 \times 10^{-19}}{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}} = 2{\cdot}65\ \mathrm{eV}\)

**(ii) The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron.**

Einstein's photoelectric equation:

\(K_{\max} = E - \phi_0 = 2{\cdot}65 - 2{\cdot}31\)

\(K_{\max} = 0{\cdot}34\ \mathrm{eV} = 5{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-20}\ \mathrm{J}\)

**(iii) The stopping potential.**

The stopping potential is the retarding voltage that just turns back the fastest electron, so \(eV_0 = K_{\max}\):

\(V_0 = \dfrac{K_{\max}}{e} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}34\ \mathrm{eV}}{e}\)

\(V_0 = 0{\cdot}34\ \mathrm{V}\)

**Why the last step looks like no step at all.** The arithmetic is a division by \(e\), and the answer comes out numerically identical to \(K_{\max}\) in electronvolts. That is not a coincidence but the definition of the electronvolt: an energy of \(n\) eV divided by \(e\) is a potential of \(n\) volts. Working the whole question in electronvolts rather than joules therefore makes part (iii) free — and it is the reason photoelectric questions are set in those units.

**A check on the numbers.** \(E\) exceeds \(\phi_0\) by only \(0{\cdot}34\) eV, so this light is barely above threshold. The threshold frequency is

\(\nu_0 = \dfrac{\phi_0}{h} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}31 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}}{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}} \approx 5{\cdot}6 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}\)

comfortably below the \(6{\cdot}4 \times 10^{14}\) Hz supplied, so emission does occur — as the question states.

rows.stem:
A beam of light consisting of two wavelengths 600 nm and 500 nm is used in a Young's double slit experiment. The slit separation is 1.0 mm and the screen is kept 0.60 m away from the plane of the slits. Calculate :
(i) the distance of the second bright fringe from the central maximum for wavelength 500 nm, and
(ii) the least distance from the central maximum where the bright fringes due to both the wavelengths coincide.
rows.solution:
Here \(d = 1{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{mm} = 10^{-3}\) m and \(D = 0{\cdot}60\) m, and the position of the \(n\)th bright fringe is

\(x_n = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}\)

**(i) The second bright fringe for \(\lambda = 500\) nm.**

\(x_2 = \dfrac{2 \times 500 \times 10^{-9} \times 0{\cdot}60}{10^{-3}}\)

\(x_2 = 6{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m} = 0{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{mm}\)

**(ii) Where the two patterns first coincide.**

Two patterns are superposed on the same screen, one with fringe spacing \(\beta_1 = \lambda_1 D/d\) for \(600\) nm and one with \(\beta_2\) for \(500\) nm. A point is bright in **both** when some bright fringe of one falls exactly on a bright fringe of the other:

\(n_1\lambda_1 = n_2\lambda_2\)

\(n_1 \times 600 = n_2 \times 500 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{n_1}{n_2} = \dfrac{500}{600} = \dfrac{5}{6}\)

The **least** such position takes the smallest whole numbers in that ratio, so \(n_1 = 5\) and \(n_2 = 6\): the 5th bright fringe of the \(600\) nm light lands on the 6th of the \(500\) nm light.

\(x = \dfrac{5 \times 600 \times 10^{-9} \times 0{\cdot}60}{10^{-3}} = 1{\cdot}8 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}\)

**\(x = 1{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{mm}\)**

Checking it the other way, which is the point of the condition:

\(\dfrac{6 \times 500 \times 10^{-9} \times 0{\cdot}60}{10^{-3}} = 1{\cdot}8 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}\)

The same place, as it must be.

**What the screen looks like.** Only the central maximum is common to both colours at \(x = 0\); on either side the two sets of fringes drift steadily out of step, overlapping into coloured bands, and they come back into register for the first time at \(1{\cdot}8\) mm. After that the coincidences repeat every \(1{\cdot}8\) mm, at \(n_1 = 10, 15, \ldots\) — coincidence positions are an arithmetic sequence, not a thinning-out one.

rows.subtopic: Atomic Masses and Composition of the Nucleus
rows.stem:
(a) James Chadwick, in 1932, studied the emission of neutral radiations when Beryllium nuclei were bombarded with alpha particles. He concluded that emitted radiations were neutrons and not photons. Explain.
(b) Two nuclei may have the same radius, even though they contain different number of protons and neutrons. Explain.
rows.solution:
**(a) Why Chadwick's neutral radiation could not be photons.**

Bombarding beryllium with alpha particles released something electrically neutral — it left no track in a cloud chamber and was undeflected by electric and magnetic fields. The obvious candidate was a gamma-ray photon. Chadwick ruled it out on **energy grounds**.

He let the unknown radiation strike paraffin and measured the energy of the protons knocked out of it. Then he asked what photon energy would be needed to give a proton that much energy in a head-on collision, applying conservation of **both energy and momentum**.

The answer was impossible. A photon carries momentum \(E/c\), which is very little for the energy it holds, so to hand a heavy proton a given kinetic energy the photon must carry a great deal more energy than the proton receives. The figure required came out **far larger than the energy available** from the alpha-beryllium reaction in the first place — energy would have to be created out of nothing.

A *massive* neutral particle, by contrast, explains the observations at once. A particle of mass close to the proton's transfers a large fraction of its energy in a head-on elastic collision, exactly as one billiard ball does to another, so a modest incident energy accounts for the observed proton recoils. Chadwick concluded that the radiation was a stream of new neutral particles of about the proton's mass, and named them **neutrons**:

\(^{9}_{4}\mathrm{Be} + ^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} \longrightarrow ^{12}_{6}\mathrm{C} + ^{1}_{0}n\)

The mass estimate is the decisive part of the argument. Neutrality alone was consistent with either hypothesis; only the **kinematics** separated them.

**(b) Why two different nuclei can share a radius.**

Because nuclear radius depends on the **mass number alone**:

\(R = R_0 A^{1/3}, \qquad R_0 \approx 1{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}\)

and \(A = Z + N\). The formula contains no separate \(Z\) and no separate \(N\) — only their **sum**.

So any two nuclei with the same \(A\) have the same radius, however that \(A\) is split between protons and neutrons. Such nuclei are **isobars**. For example \(^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H}\) and \(^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He}\) both have \(A = 3\) but \((Z, N) = (1, 2)\) and \((2, 1)\); \(^{40}_{18}\mathrm{Ar}\), \(^{40}_{19}\mathrm{K}\) and \(^{40}_{20}\mathrm{Ca}\) are a set of three.

**What lies behind the formula.** Since \(R \propto A^{1/3}\), the volume \(\tfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3} \propto A\), so the number of nucleons per unit volume is the **same for every nucleus**. Nuclear matter has a constant density of about \(2{\cdot}3 \times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\), which is a direct consequence of the strong nuclear force being **short-ranged and saturated**: a nucleon binds only to its immediate neighbours, not to the whole nucleus, so adding nucleons enlarges the nucleus rather than compressing it. Nucleons pack like marbles in a bag, and only how *many* there are decides the size.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem:
(a) The energy of hydrogen atom in an orbit is \(-1.51\) eV. What are kinetic and potential energies of the electron in this orbit ?
(b) The electron in a hydrogen atom is typically found at a distance of about \(5.3 \times 10^{-11}\) m from the nucleus which has a diameter of about \(1.0 \times 10^{-15}\) m. Assuming the hydrogen atom to be a sphere of radius \(5.3 \times 10^{-11}\) m, what fraction of its volume is occupied by the nucleus ?
rows.solution:
**(a) Kinetic and potential energy at \(E = -1{\cdot}51\) eV.**

For an electron bound in a hydrogen atom the three energies are locked together, whatever the orbit:

\(K = -E \qquad\text{and}\qquad U = 2E\)

so

\(K = +1{\cdot}51\ \mathrm{eV}\)

\(U = 2 \times (-1{\cdot}51) = -3{\cdot}02\ \mathrm{eV}\)

**Where those two relations come from.** Coulomb attraction supplies the centripetal force:

\(\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^{2}}{r^{2}}\)

so

\(K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^{2}}{r} \qquad\text{while}\qquad U = -\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^{2}}{r}\)

Hence \(U = -2K\) and \(E = K + U = -K\), which is the virial theorem for an inverse-square force.

Two features are worth carrying away. The kinetic energy is **positive** and equal in size to the total energy; the potential energy is **negative** and twice as large. And the total is negative, which is what *bound* means — supply \(1{\cdot}51\) eV and the electron is free.

(Incidentally \(-1{\cdot}51 = -13{\cdot}6/9\), so this is the \(n = 3\) orbit, though the question does not need it.)

**(b) The fraction of the atom's volume occupied by the nucleus.**

The nuclear **diameter** is \(1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-15}\) m, so its radius is

\(r_{\text{nucleus}} = 0{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}\)

Reading the diameter as a radius is the one trap here, and it costs a factor of eight.

Both nucleus and atom are taken as spheres, so the \(\tfrac{4}{3}\pi\) cancels and only the ratio of radii survives:

\(\dfrac{V_{\text{nucleus}}}{V_{\text{atom}}} = \dfrac{\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r_{\text{nucleus}}^{3}}{\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r_{\text{atom}}^{3}} = \left(\dfrac{r_{\text{nucleus}}}{r_{\text{atom}}}\right)^{3}\)

\(= \left(\dfrac{0{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-15}}{5{\cdot}3 \times 10^{-11}}\right)^{3} = (9{\cdot}43 \times 10^{-6})^{3}\)

\(\approx 8{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-16}\)

(The scheme prints \(8{\cdot}3 \times 10^{-16}\); the difference is rounding in the intermediate ratio, and the order of magnitude is the answer.)

**What the number means.** The nucleus holds about one part in \(10^{16}\) of the atom's volume while carrying more than \(99{\cdot}9\%\) of its mass. That is the quantitative form of Rutherford's conclusion: an atom is overwhelmingly empty space, which is exactly why most alpha particles sailed through the gold foil undeflected and only a rare one met the nucleus head-on.
